{"answer": "# Literature Review and Bayesian-Optimization Seed Data for a 15-Week LPBF Aluminium Alloy Discovery Campaign

## 1. Comprehensive Table of LPBF Aluminium Alloys

The following table summarises crack-free or near crack-free LPBF aluminium alloys spanning eutectic Al–Si baselines, Sc-containing benchmarks, Sc-free alternatives based on Al–Mn, Al–Ce, Al–Fe, Al–Cu and inoculated wrought alloys. For each system, the cracking-suppression mechanism, representative process window, as-built and heat-treated mechanical properties, relative density and critical-mineral exposure are reported. Data are drawn from peer-reviewed literature and recent reviews (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024).

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Key observations.** AlSi10Mg remains the volumetric baseline at approximately 250–350 MPa yield strength as-built, with UTS of 380–450 MPa and elongation of 5–8% (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017). Scalmalloy® achieves 456–469 MPa yield strength after direct aging at 325 °C for 4 h, but relies on ~0.7 wt% Sc (pqac-00000001). Among Sc-free systems, the Al–Mn–Ti–Zr alloy by Mair et al. achieved 284 MPa yield strength and 16.9% elongation as-built through metastable Mn supersaturation and coherent L1₂ Al₃(Ti,Zr) grain refinement (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000024). The A20X-type Al–Cu–TiB₂ alloy reached 401 MPa UTS as-built with 17.7% elongation and 99.5% density, with TiB₂ providing heterogeneous nucleation and sub-micron grain size (pqac-00000005). Near-eutectic Al–10Ce delivered 222 MPa yield strength and 319 MPa UTS with 10.8% elongation, exploiting the thermally stable Al₁₁Ce₃ eutectic (pqac-00000006). Al–Fe–Mg–Zr eutectic alloys reached 376 MPa yield strength after aging at 400 °C for 4 h (pqac-00000022), and Al–Fe–Cr quasicrystal-reinforced composites reached 395 MPa yield strength and 531 MPa UTS, though with limited ductility (pqac-00000023). For inoculated wrought alloys, AA7075 + 1 wt% Zr achieved crack-free builds with 325–373 MPa yield strength (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010), and AA6061 + Zr-based nanoparticles reached 267 MPa UTS with 14.2% elongation and 99.94% density (pqac-00000010).

---

## 2. Recommended Literature-Chosen Seed Compositions

For a campaign whose search space covers Al with additions from {Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce}, four seed compositions are recommended that (i) spread across the composition space, (ii) are dosable from available master alloys and elemental additions, (iii) melt fully at moderate superheat, and (iv) are likely printable without a heated plate:

**Seed 1: Al–10Si–0.35Mg (AlSi10Mg baseline).** This eutectic system is universally printable, requires no heated plate, melts at ~600 °C with minimal superheat, and is dosable from elemental Si and Mg. It anchors the Si-rich corner and serves as the density and cracking benchmark. Extensive literature data exist for model validation (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017).

**Seed 2: Al–4Mn–0.5Ti–0.5Zr (~Mair-type).** Dosable from Al–10Mn, Al–10Ti and Al–10Zr master alloys. The liquidus is only moderately elevated by Mn, Ti and Zr additions (Mn has ~2 wt% equilibrium solubility at ~660 °C, and Ti/Zr additions are small). The alloy prints crack-free without preheat at 380 W / 1900 mm/s with 284 MPa yield strength and excellent 16.9% elongation (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000024). This anchors the Mn-rich, Sc-free transition-metal corner.

**Seed 3: Al–10Ce (near-eutectic).** Dosable from Al–10Ce master alloy. The Al–Ce eutectic at ~10 wt% Ce melts near 640 °C with high fluidity and a narrow freezing range, ensuring crack-free printing without preheat (pqac-00000006). The composition anchors the rare-earth/eutectic corner and provides thermal stability data. Ce is a rare-earth element but substantially more abundant and less supply-critical than Sc or Er.

**Seed 4: Al–4.5Cu–0.3Mg–0.3Ti + 1 vol% TiB₂ (A20X-type).** Dosable from elemental Cu, Mg and Al–Ti–B master alloy or pre-alloyed A20X powder. This anchors the Cu-rich, age-hardenable corner. The TiB₂ grain-refinement strategy produces crack-free, dense parts with 401 MPa UTS and 17.7% elongation as-built (pqac-00000005). The liquidus is below ~650 °C and the alloy prints without preheat.

These four seeds cover the Si, Mn/Cr/Zr, Ce/Fe/Ni and Cu corners of the accessible search space. They avoid clustering, are all achievable by ultrasonic atomization from a 6063 or high-purity Al base with master-alloy dosing, and have demonstrated printability without heated plates.

---

## 3. Atomization Problems and Composition Fidelity

**Droplet size prediction.** For ultrasonic atomization of aluminium alloys at typical operating frequencies of 20–60 kHz, the characteristic droplet diameter can be estimated via the Lang-type relation D₃₂ ≈ 0.34·[8πγ/(ρf²)]^(1/3), where γ is the melt surface tension, ρ is the density and f is the ultrasonic frequency. Corrections based on Weber, Ohnesorge and intensity numbers refine the estimate. Doubling frequency is predicted to reduce powder size by approximately 40% (pqac-00000018). Accuracy is typically ±20–30% for metals when thermophysical properties are well known.

**Mg and Zn evaporation.** Magnesium (boiling point ~1091 °C) and zinc (boiling point ~907 °C) are volatile under the temperatures needed to melt aluminium alloys for atomization and during LPBF processing. Mg loss of 0.5–2 wt% is commonly observed during both gas atomization and LPBF, reducing the effectiveness of Mg₂Si and MgZn₂ precipitation strengthening (pqac-00000019). For alloys targeting >4 wt% Mg (Addalloy-type or Scalmalloy compositions), significant process-stability problems arise from Mg evaporation and spatter during LPBF, which Mair et al. noted as a key reason to favor the Al–Mn system over Al–Mg for Sc-free designs (pqac-00000024). Zn is even more volatile and losses can exceed 1–3 wt% during LPBF, making 7xxx-type compositions especially challenging for composition fidelity.

**Oxide films.** Aluminium readily forms Al₂O₃ films. In small-batch ultrasonic atomization, maintaining inert-atmosphere purity (<100 ppm O₂) is essential. Oxide films on powders increase laser reflectivity, reduce flowability and can create oxide inclusions in printed parts. Charge sizes of 250 g are small enough that oxide-to-volume ratio may be higher than in industrial-scale atomization.

**Primary intermetallics.** High Zr content (>~0.5 wt%) risks formation of primary Al₃Zr during slow cooling of the melt before atomization, which can clog nozzles and produce inhomogeneous powder. The peritectic nature of Al₃Zr (formation at ~660 °C) means that at >1 wt% Zr, significant primary particles form unless extremely rapid quenching occurs. Similarly, Cr has very limited solubility in Al (~0.4 wt% at 660 °C) and can form primary Al₇Cr or Al₁₃Cr₂ intermetallics. Ce and Ni form intermetallics (Al₁₁Ce₃, Al₃Ni) at eutectic compositions, which are actually beneficial for printability but may settle or segregate in the crucible before atomization if the melt superheat is insufficient.

**Composition fidelity expectations.** For the recommended seed compositions atomized in 250 g batches: (i) Si, Cu, Fe, Ni and Ce are expected to be retained within ±0.2 wt% of target; (ii) Mn, Ti, Zr and Cr within ±0.3 wt% if well-dissolved; (iii) Mg within ±0.5–1.0 wt% due to evaporation; (iv) Zn may lose 1–3 wt%. ICP-OES verification of every powder batch is essential.

---

## 4. Open Datasets and Databases for Seeding the BO Pipeline

The following table summarizes available experimental compilations, repositories and CALPHAD resources for initializing both the process-parameter and property stages of the Bayesian-optimization pipeline.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Process-stage seeding.** The NIST AM-Bench 2022 aluminium challenge data provides single-track absorptance and X-ray imaging data for laser melting of bare aluminium plate, useful for calibrating melt-pool models (pqac-00000011). The Barrionuevo et al. AlSi10Mg compilation reportedly aggregates ~270 records spanning laser power, speed, hatch, layer thickness, preheat, density, hardness and tensile properties from multiple studies, providing a useful structured dataset for process–density and process–property surrogate models. Machine-learning-optimized process parameter data for AlSi10Mg (200–355 W, 1307–2320 mm/s, relative densities of 99.2–99.4%) have been reported with Gaussian process regression achieving high accuracy (pqac-00000015).

**Property-stage seeding.** Review articles by Aversa et al. (2019) and Liu et al. (2024) contain tabulated tensile data for 10–30+ LPBF Al alloys covering compositions, process conditions, microstructures and mechanical properties, which can be manually digitized for training (pqac-00000016). CALPHAD databases (Thermo-Calc TCAL, Pandat PanAl) can generate arbitrarily large synthetic composition screens of Scheil curves, phase fractions and thermophysical properties for use as low-fidelity training data (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029).

---

## 5. Physics-Based and Semi-Empirical Models for Synthetic Data Generation

The following table details models that can generate low-cost "fantasy" data for each stage of the BO pipeline, their accuracy for LPBF aluminium, and how they have been used as priors or low-fidelity sources.

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

**Melt-pool models (Eagar–Tsai, Rosenthal).** The Eagar–Tsai model treats the laser as a moving Gaussian heat source on a semi-infinite body and predicts melt-pool width, depth and temperature field. It is typically accurate to ±20–30% for conduction-mode LPBF after alloy-specific absorptivity calibration, but fails in the keyhole regime because it neglects recoil pressure, Marangoni convection and free-surface depression. McElfresh et al. (2024) used the Eagar–Tsai model as a fast surrogate within a cellular-automaton framework for LPBF microstructure prediction. Lack-of-fusion criteria (pool depth ≥ layer thickness with overlap) and keyhole thresholds (normalized enthalpy or aspect ratio) can be applied to the model outputs to delineate admissible process windows. For LPBF 6061 aluminium, Sonawane (2021) coupled Rosenthal thermal simulations with the RDG hot-cracking criterion and found qualitative agreement between predicted cracking-sensitivity maps and experimental observations (pqac-00000012).

**Scheil-based hot-cracking indices.** The Kou index, defined as |dT/d(f_s^{1/2})| near complete solidification, computed from Scheil–Gulliver curves using CALPHAD databases, has shown good qualitative correlation with experimental LPBF cracking behaviour for binary Al–Si, Al–Mg and Al–Cu alloys (pqac-00000013). Hyer et al. (2020) demonstrated that including solid-state diffusion in the Scheil simulation substantially reduces predicted susceptibility and shifts the composition of maximum susceptibility. The Clyne–Davies CSC and Scheil-based brittle-temperature-range (BTR) criteria provide complementary metrics. Dreano et al. (2022) used a genetic algorithm with Scheil-BTR minimization and solid-solution strengthening maximization to computationally design a crack-free Al–6.7Mg–3Si–1.4Ni–1Zn–0.3Fe alloy with a BTR of only 9 °C (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). Uba et al. (2025) used Kou's HSI criterion and Clyne–Davies CSC in Thermo-Calc to screen modified Al 7xxx compositions for LPBF printability (pqac-00000030).

**Strengthening models.** Solid-solution strengthening using an atomic-size-misfit power law (Δσ_ss ∝ K·ε^{4/3}·c^{2/3}) was applied by Dreano et al. for alloy optimization (pqac-00000027). For the Al–Mn–Ti–Zr system, Mair et al. measured that 3.7 wt% Mn in supersaturated solid solution contributed approximately 104 MPa (37% of the 284 MPa yield strength), consistent with the ~30 MPa per wt% Mn literature value (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000024). Orowan precipitation strengthening has been used to predict the aging response of L1₂ Al₃(Sc,Zr) precipitates in Scalmalloy-type alloys and of quasicrystalline particles in Al–Fe–Cr composites (pqac-00000023). Taheri-Mousavi et al. (2024) used a hybrid ICME + Bayesian-optimization workflow with CALPHAD-derived descriptors including L1₂ phase fraction, coarsening metrics and cracking susceptibility as inputs to a neural-network surrogate, achieving ~3% normalized prediction error with 40 training compositions and using expected-improvement Bayesian optimization to identify an optimized Al–Er–Zr–Ni alloy with 40% higher L1₂ fraction than the initial design (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

**Lang's equation for ultrasonic atomization.** The simplified Lang relation D ≈ 0.34·[8πγ/(ρf²)]^{1/3} predicts the Sauter mean droplet diameter from melt surface tension γ, density ρ and ultrasonic frequency f, with corrections for Weber, Ohnesorge and intensity numbers (pqac-00000018). Accuracy is approximately ±20–30% for metals. This can seed an atomization-stage BO model predicting sieve yield and particle size distribution as a function of frequency, temperature and composition.

---

## References

Among Sc-free systems, the Al–Mn–Ti–Zr alloy by Mair et al. achieved 284 MPa yield strength and 16.9% elongation as-built through metastable Mn supersaturation and coherent L1₂ Al₃(Ti,Zr) grain refinement (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000024). The A20X-type Al–Cu–TiB₂ alloy reached 401 MPa UTS as-built with 17.7% elongation and 99.5% density, with TiB₂ providing heterogeneous nucleation and sub-micron grain size (pqac-00000005). Near-eutectic Al–10Ce delivered 222 MPa yield strength and 319 MPa UTS with 10.8% elongation, exploiting the thermally stable Al₁₁Ce₃ eutectic (pqac-00000006). Al–Fe–Mg–Zr eutectic alloys reached 376 MPa yield strength after aging at 400 °C for 4 h (pqac-00000022), and Al–Fe–Cr quasicrystal-reinforced composites reached 395 MPa yield strength and 531 MPa UTS, though with limited ductility (pqac-00000023). For inoculated wrought alloys, AA7075 + 1 wt% Zr achieved crack-free builds with 325–373 MPa yield strength (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010), and AA6061 + Zr-based nanoparticles reached 267 MPa UTS with 14.2% elongation and 99.94% density (pqac-00000010).

---

## 2. Recommended Literature-Chosen Seed Compositions

For a campaign whose search space covers Al with additions from {Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce}, four seed compositions are recommended that (i) spread across the composition space, (ii) are dosable from available master alloys and elemental additions, (iii) melt fully at moderate superheat, and (iv) are likely printable without a heated plate:

**Seed 1: Al–10Si–0.35Mg (AlSi10Mg baseline).** This eutectic system is universally printable, requires no heated plate, melts at ~600 °C with minimal superheat, and is dosable from elemental Si and Mg. It anchors the Si-rich corner and serves as the density and cracking benchmark. Extensive literature data exist for model validation (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017).

**Seed 2: Al–4Mn–0.5Ti–0.5Zr (~Mair-type).** Dosable from Al–10Mn, Al–10Ti and Al–10Zr master alloys. The liquidus is only moderately elevated by Mn, Ti and Zr additions (Mn has ~2 wt% equilibrium solubility at ~660 °C, and Ti/Zr additions are small). The alloy prints crack-free without preheat at 380 W / 1900 mm/s with 284 MPa yield strength and excellent 16.9% elongation (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000024). This anchors the Mn-rich, Sc-free transition-metal corner.

**Seed 3: Al–10Ce (near-eutectic).** Dosable from Al–10Ce master alloy. The Al–Ce eutectic at ~10 wt% Ce melts near 640 °C with high fluidity and a narrow freezing range, ensuring crack-free printing without preheat (pqac-00000006). The composition anchors the rare-earth/eutectic corner and provides thermal stability data. Ce is a rare-earth element but substantially more abundant and less supply-critical than Sc or Er.

**Seed 4: Al–4.5Cu–0.3Mg–0.3Ti + 1 vol% TiB₂ (A20X-type).** Dosable from elemental Cu, Mg and Al–Ti–B master alloy or pre-alloyed A20X powder. This anchors the Cu-rich, age-hardenable corner. The TiB₂ grain-refinement strategy produces crack-free, dense parts with 401 MPa UTS and 17.7% elongation as-built (pqac-00000005). The liquidus is below ~650 °C and the alloy prints without preheat.

These four seeds cover the Si, Mn/Cr/Zr, Ce/Fe/Ni and Cu corners of the accessible search space. They avoid clustering, are all achievable by ultrasonic atomization from a 6063 or high-purity Al base with master-alloy dosing, and have demonstrated printability without heated plates.

---

## 3. Atomization Problems and Composition Fidelity

**Droplet size prediction.** For ultrasonic atomization of aluminium alloys at typical operating frequencies of 20–60 kHz, the characteristic droplet diameter can be estimated via the Lang-type relation D₃₂ ≈ 0.34·[8πγ/(ρf²)]^(1/3), where γ is the melt surface tension, ρ is the density and f is the ultrasonic frequency. Corrections based on Weber, Ohnesorge and intensity numbers refine the estimate. Doubling frequency is predicted to reduce powder size by approximately 40% (pqac-00000018). Accuracy is typically ±20–30% for metals when thermophysical properties are well known.

**Mg and Zn evaporation.** Magnesium (boiling point ~1091 °C) and zinc (boiling point ~907 °C) are volatile under the temperatures needed to melt aluminium alloys for atomization and during LPBF processing. Mg loss of 0.5–2 wt% is commonly observed during both gas atomization and LPBF, reducing the effectiveness of Mg₂Si and MgZn₂ precipitation strengthening (pqac-00000019). For alloys targeting >4 wt% Mg (Addalloy-type or Scalmalloy compositions), significant process-stability problems arise from Mg evaporation and spatter during LPBF, which Mair et al. noted as a key reason to favor the Al–Mn system over Al–Mg for Sc-free designs (pqac-00000024). Zn is even more volatile and losses can exceed 1–3 wt% during LPBF, making 7xxx-type compositions especially challenging for composition fidelity.

**Oxide films.** Aluminium readily forms Al₂O₃ films. In small-batch ultrasonic atomization, maintaining inert-atmosphere purity (<100 ppm O₂) is essential. Oxide films on powders increase laser reflectivity, reduce flowability and can create oxide inclusions in printed parts. Charge sizes of 250 g are small enough that oxide-to-volume ratio may be higher than in industrial-scale atomization.

**Primary intermetallics.** High Zr content (>~0.5 wt%) risks formation of primary Al₃Zr during slow cooling of the melt before atomization, which can clog nozzles and produce inhomogeneous powder. The peritectic nature of Al₃Zr (formation at ~660 °C) means that at >1 wt% Zr, significant primary particles form unless extremely rapid quenching occurs. Similarly, Cr has very limited solubility in Al (~0.4 wt% at 660 °C) and can form primary Al₇Cr or Al₁₃Cr₂ intermetallics. Ce and Ni form intermetallics (Al₁₁Ce₃, Al₃Ni) at eutectic compositions, which are actually beneficial for printability but may settle or segregate in the crucible before atomization if the melt superheat is insufficient.

**Composition fidelity expectations.** For the recommended seed compositions atomized in 250 g batches: (i) Si, Cu, Fe, Ni and Ce are expected to be retained within ±0.2 wt% of target; (ii) Mn, Ti, Zr and Cr within ±0.3 wt% if well-dissolved; (iii) Mg within ±0.5–1.0 wt% due to evaporation; (iv) Zn may lose 1–3 wt%. ICP-OES verification of every powder batch is essential.

---

## 4. Open Datasets and Databases for Seeding the BO Pipeline

The following table summarizes available experimental compilations, repositories and CALPHAD resources for initializing both the process-parameter and property stages of the Bayesian-optimization pipeline.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Process-stage seeding.** The NIST AM-Bench 2022 aluminium challenge data provides single-track absorptance and X-ray imaging data for laser melting of bare aluminium plate, useful for calibrating melt-pool models (pqac-00000011). The Barrionuevo et al. AlSi10Mg compilation reportedly aggregates ~270 records spanning laser power, speed, hatch, layer thickness, preheat, density, hardness and tensile properties from multiple studies, providing a useful structured dataset for process–density and process–property surrogate models. Machine-learning-optimized process parameter data for AlSi10Mg (200–355 W, 1307–2320 mm/s, relative densities of 99.2–99.4%) have been reported with Gaussian process regression achieving high accuracy (pqac-00000015).

**Property-stage seeding.** Review articles by Aversa et al. (2019) and Liu et al. (2024) contain tabulated tensile data for 10–30+ LPBF Al alloys covering compositions, process conditions, microstructures and mechanical properties, which can be manually digitized for training (pqac-00000016). CALPHAD databases (Thermo-Calc TCAL, Pandat PanAl) can generate arbitrarily large synthetic composition screens of Scheil curves, phase fractions and thermophysical properties for use as low-fidelity training data (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029).

---

## 5. Physics-Based and Semi-Empirical Models for Synthetic Data Generation

The following table details models that can generate low-cost "fantasy" data for each stage of the BO pipeline, their accuracy for LPBF aluminium, and how they have been used as priors or low-fidelity sources.

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

**Melt-pool models (Eagar–Tsai, Rosenthal).** The Eagar–Tsai model treats the laser as a moving Gaussian heat source on a semi-infinite body and predicts melt-pool width, depth and temperature field. It is typically accurate to ±20–30% for conduction-mode LPBF after alloy-specific absorptivity calibration, but fails in the keyhole regime because it neglects recoil pressure, Marangoni convection and free-surface depression. McElfresh et al. (2024) used the Eagar–Tsai model as a fast surrogate within a cellular-automaton framework for LPBF microstructure prediction. Lack-of-fusion criteria (pool depth ≥ layer thickness with overlap) and keyhole thresholds (normalized enthalpy or aspect ratio) can be applied to the model outputs to delineate admissible process windows. For LPBF 6061 aluminium, Sonawane (2021) coupled Rosenthal thermal simulations with the RDG hot-cracking criterion and found qualitative agreement between predicted cracking-sensitivity maps and experimental observations (pqac-00000012).

**Scheil-based hot-cracking indices.** The Kou index, defined as |dT/d(f_s^{1/2})| near complete solidification, computed from Scheil–Gulliver curves using CALPHAD databases, has shown good qualitative correlation with experimental LPBF cracking behaviour for binary Al–Si, Al–Mg and Al–Cu alloys (pqac-00000013). Hyer et al. (2020) demonstrated that including solid-state diffusion in the Scheil simulation substantially reduces predicted susceptibility and shifts the composition of maximum susceptibility. The Clyne–Davies CSC and Scheil-based brittle-temperature-range (BTR) criteria provide complementary metrics. Dreano et al. (2022) used a genetic algorithm with Scheil-BTR minimization and solid-solution strengthening maximization to computationally design a crack-free Al–6.7Mg–3Si–1.4Ni–1Zn–0.3Fe alloy with a BTR of only 9 °C (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). Uba et al. (2025) used Kou's HSI criterion and Clyne–Davies CSC in Thermo-Calc to screen modified Al 7xxx compositions for LPBF printability (pqac-00000030).

**Strengthening models.** Solid-solution strengthening using an atomic-size-misfit power law (Δσ_ss ∝ K·ε^{4/3}·c^{2/3}) was applied by Dreano et al. for alloy optimization (pqac-00000027). For the Al–Mn–Ti–Zr system, Mair et al. measured that 3.7 wt% Mn in supersaturated solid solution contributed approximately 104 MPa (37% of the 284 MPa yield strength), consistent with the ~30 MPa per wt% Mn literature value (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000024). Orowan precipitation strengthening has been used to predict the aging response of L1₂ Al₃(Sc,Zr) precipitates in Scalmalloy-type alloys and of quasicrystalline particles in Al–Fe–Cr composites (pqac-00000023). Taheri-Mousavi et al. (2024) used a hybrid ICME + Bayesian-optimization workflow with CALPHAD-derived descriptors including L1₂ phase fraction, coarsening metrics and cracking susceptibility as inputs to a neural-network surrogate, achieving ~3% normalized prediction error with 40 training compositions and using expected-improvement Bayesian optimization to identify an optimized Al–Er–Zr–Ni alloy with 40% higher L1₂ fraction than the initial design (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

**Lang's equation for ultrasonic atomization.** The simplified Lang relation D ≈ 0.34·[8πγ/(ρf²)]^{1/3} predicts the Sauter mean droplet diameter from melt surface tension γ, density ρ and ultrasonic frequency f, with corrections for Weber, Ohnesorge and intensity numbers (pqac-00000018). Accuracy is approximately ±20–30% for metals. This can seed an atomization-stage BO model predicting sieve yield and particle size distribution as a function of frequency, temperature and composition.

---

state.question:
For a 15-week laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) aluminium alloy discovery campaign we need (a) a short list of known alloys to use as baselines and as literature-chosen seed compositions, and (b) published data and cheap models to seed each stage of a Bayesian-optimization pipeline before our own experiments exist.

CONTEXT
Our alloys are made by ultrasonic atomization of 250 g charges from a 6063 or high-purity Al base with additions from Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn and Sn (at least 85 at.% Al, a few additions per alloy, dosed as master alloys or elemental powders). They are then printed as single tracks, small cubes and sub-size tensile bars on a research LPBF machine (Aconity MIDI class, 400 W-class fibre laser), with and without a heated plate. Goal: beat LPBF AlSi10Mg on yield strength and/or approach Scalmalloy (Al-Mg-Sc-Zr) with much less Sc or other critical minerals. Benchmarks: AlSi10Mg and Scalmalloy.

Please review the peer-reviewed literature and give:
1. A table of LPBF aluminium alloys that are Sc-free or Sc-lean and print crack-free, with nominal composition (wt% and at.%), how cracking was suppressed (eutectic fraction, Zr/Ti/Er/TiB2 inoculation, etc.), the process window (laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness, plate preheat, volumetric energy density), as-built and heat-treated yield strength, UTS and elongation, relative density, and DOIs. Cover at least: AlSi10Mg, AlSi7Mg and AlSi12; Scalmalloy and lower-Sc Al-Mg-Sc-Zr; Al-Mg-Zr (Addalloy-type); Al-Mn-Sc and Al-Mn-Cr-Zr; Al-Zr and Al-Zr-Er/Yb; Al-Ce(-Mn, -Ni, -Mg); Al-Fe and Al-Fe-Ni / Al-Ni-Zr; Al-Cu-Mg with Zr, Ti or TiB2 (A20X-type, 2024+Zr); 6061 and 7075 with Zr or Ti/TiB2 inoculation; Al-Mg-Si with Zr. Flag which ones use critical minerals (Sc, Er and other rare earths, Li, etc.).
2. Which 3-4 of these make the best literature-chosen seeds for a campaign whose search space covers compositions near these systems, given that they should (i) spread out over the space rather than cluster, (ii) be dosable from master alloys (Al-Zr, Al-Mn, Al-Cr, Al-Ce, Al-Er, Al-Ti) and elemental Si, Mg, Cu, Fe and Ni, (iii) melt fully in a small crucible at moderate superheat (consider liquidus rise from Zr and Cr, primary Al3Zr at high Zr, Ce/Fe/Ni intermetallics), and (iv) be likely printable without a heated plate. Give specific compositions and the reasons.
3. Known problems when atomizing these compositions in small batches (Mg and Zn evaporation, oxide films, primary intermetallics of Zr or Cr, segregation) and the composition fidelity to expect.
4. Open datasets or databases of LPBF aluminium data that could seed (a) a print-parameter stage (laser power, speed, hatch, layer -> relative density, melt-pool size, cracking) and (b) a property stage (composition, process and heat treatment -> hardness, yield strength, UTS, elongation). For example: compiled LPBF Al process-density datasets, NIST AM-Bench, the Barrionuevo et al. data descriptor, Materials Data Facility, Citrine, Zenodo or Figshare datasets, review articles with tabulated LPBF Al tensile data, and aluminium alloy property databases used for machine learning. For each give the size, the variables, the licence or access model, and the DOI or URL.
5. Physics-based or semi-empirical models that can generate synthetic ("fantasy") pre-experiment data for each stage at low cost: Eagar-Tsai or Rosenthal melt-pool models with lack-of-fusion and keyhole criteria for print windows; Scheil-based hot-cracking indices (Kou index, CSC) from CALPHAD; solid-solution, precipitation (L1_2, Orowan) and grain-boundary strengthening models for yield strength; and droplet-size relations for ultrasonic atomization (e.g., Lang's relation). How accurate are they for LPBF aluminium, and how have they been used as priors or low-fidelity sources in Bayesian optimization?

Give a reference list with DOIs.

**Key observations.** AlSi10Mg remains the volumetric baseline at approximately 250–350 MPa yield strength as-built, with UTS of 380–450 MPa and elongation of 5–8% (he2021designanddevelopment pages 30-35, li2026designinnovationsand pages 5-7). Scalmalloy® achieves 456–469 MPa yield strength after direct aging at 325 °C for 4 h, but relies on ~0.7 wt% Sc (cerri2024mainheattreatments pages 1-2). Among Sc-free systems, the Al–Mn–Ti–Zr alloy by Mair et al. achieved 284 MPa yield strength and 16.9% elongation as-built through metastable Mn supersaturation and coherent L1₂ Al₃(Ti,Zr) grain refinement (mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 1-2). The A20X-type Al–Cu–TiB₂ alloy reached 401 MPa UTS as-built with 17.7% elongation and 99.5% density, with TiB₂ providing heterogeneous nucleation and sub-micron grain size (mair2021microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2). Near-eutectic Al–10Ce delivered 222 MPa yield strength and 319 MPa UTS with 10.8% elongation, exploiting the thermally stable Al₁₁Ce₃ eutectic (hesselmann2022effectofprecipitationforming pages 1-3). Al–Fe–Mg–Zr eutectic alloys reached 376 MPa yield strength after aging at 400 °C for 4 h (li2025precipitationevolutionaging pages 1-3), and Al–Fe–Cr quasicrystal-reinforced composites reached 395 MPa yield strength and 531 MPa UTS, though with limited ductility (kang2023laserpowderbed pages 1-3). For inoculated wrought alloys, AA7075 + 1 wt% Zr achieved crack-free builds with 325–373 MPa yield strength (yu2022processingandcharacterization pages 1-2, hussain2026metallurgicalaspectsof pages 7-8), and AA6061 + Zr-based nanoparticles reached 267 MPa UTS with 14.2% elongation and 99.94% density (hussain2026metallurgicalaspectsof pages 7-8).

## 2. Recommended Literature-Chosen Seed Compositions

For a campaign whose search space covers Al with additions from {Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce}, four seed compositions are recommended that (i) spread across the composition space, (ii) are dosable from available master alloys and elemental additions, (iii) melt fully at moderate superheat, and (iv) are likely printable without a heated plate:

**Seed 1: Al–10Si–0.35Mg (AlSi10Mg baseline).** This eutectic system is universally printable, requires no heated plate, melts at ~600 °C with minimal superheat, and is dosable from elemental Si and Mg. It anchors the Si-rich corner and serves as the density and cracking benchmark. Extensive literature data exist for model validation (he2021designanddevelopment pages 30-35, li2026designinnovationsand pages 5-7).

**Seed 2: Al–4Mn–0.5Ti–0.5Zr (~Mair-type).** Dosable from Al–10Mn, Al–10Ti and Al–10Zr master alloys. The liquidus is only moderately elevated by Mn, Ti and Zr additions (Mn has ~2 wt% equilibrium solubility at ~660 °C, and Ti/Zr additions are small). The alloy prints crack-free without preheat at 380 W / 1900 mm/s with 284 MPa yield strength and excellent 16.9% elongation (mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 1-2). This anchors the Mn-rich, Sc-free transition-metal corner.

**Seed 3: Al–10Ce (near-eutectic).** Dosable from Al–10Ce master alloy. The Al–Ce eutectic at ~10 wt% Ce melts near 640 °C with high fluidity and a narrow freezing range, ensuring crack-free printing without preheat (hesselmann2022effectofprecipitationforming pages 1-3). The composition anchors the rare-earth/eutectic corner and provides thermal stability data. Ce is a rare-earth element but substantially more abundant and less supply-critical than Sc or Er.

**Seed 4: Al–4.5Cu–0.3Mg–0.3Ti + 1 vol% TiB₂ (A20X-type).** Dosable from elemental Cu, Mg and Al–Ti–B master alloy or pre-alloyed A20X powder. This anchors the Cu-rich, age-hardenable corner. The TiB₂ grain-refinement strategy produces crack-free, dense parts with 401 MPa UTS and 17.7% elongation as-built (mair2021microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2). The liquidus is below ~650 °C and the alloy prints without preheat.

These four seeds cover the Si, Mn/Cr/Zr, Ce/Fe/Ni and Cu corners of the accessible search space. They avoid clustering, are all achievable by ultrasonic atomization from a 6063 or high-purity Al base with master-alloy dosing, and have demonstrated printability without heated plates.

## 3. Atomization Problems and Composition Fidelity

**Droplet size prediction.** For ultrasonic atomization of aluminium alloys at typical operating frequencies of 20–60 kHz, the characteristic droplet diameter can be estimated via the Lang-type relation D₃₂ ≈ 0.34·[8πγ/(ρf²)]^(1/3), where γ is the melt surface tension, ρ is the density and f is the ultrasonic frequency. Corrections based on Weber, Ohnesorge and intensity numbers refine the estimate. Doubling frequency is predicted to reduce powder size by approximately 40% (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 4-5). Accuracy is typically ±20–30% for metals when thermophysical properties are well known.

**Mg and Zn evaporation.** Magnesium (boiling point ~1091 °C) and zinc (boiling point ~907 °C) are volatile under the temperatures needed to melt aluminium alloys for atomization and during LPBF processing. Mg loss of 0.5–2 wt% is commonly observed during both gas atomization and LPBF, reducing the effectiveness of Mg₂Si and MgZn₂ precipitation strengthening (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 38-42). For alloys targeting >4 wt% Mg (Addalloy-type or Scalmalloy compositions), significant process-stability problems arise from Mg evaporation and spatter during LPBF, which Mair et al. noted as a key reason to favor the Al–Mn system over Al–Mg for Sc-free designs (mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 1-2). Zn is even more volatile and losses can exceed 1–3 wt% during LPBF, making 7xxx-type compositions especially challenging for composition fidelity.

**Oxide films.** Aluminium readily forms Al₂O₃ films. In small-batch ultrasonic atomization, maintaining inert-atmosphere purity (<100 ppm O₂) is essential. Oxide films on powders increase laser reflectivity, reduce flowability and can create oxide inclusions in printed parts. Charge sizes of 250 g are small enough that oxide-to-volume ratio may be higher than in industrial-scale atomization.

**Primary intermetallics.** High Zr content (>~0.5 wt%) risks formation of primary Al₃Zr during slow cooling of the melt before atomization, which can clog nozzles and produce inhomogeneous powder. The peritectic nature of Al₃Zr (formation at ~660 °C) means that at >1 wt% Zr, significant primary particles form unless extremely rapid quenching occurs. Similarly, Cr has very limited solubility in Al (~0.4 wt% at 660 °C) and can form primary Al₇Cr or Al₁₃Cr₂ intermetallics. Ce and Ni form intermetallics (Al₁₁Ce₃, Al₃Ni) at eutectic compositions, which are actually beneficial for printability but may settle or segregate in the crucible before atomization if the melt superheat is insufficient.

**Composition fidelity expectations.** For the recommended seed compositions atomized in 250 g batches: (i) Si, Cu, Fe, Ni and Ce are expected to be retained within ±0.2 wt% of target; (ii) Mn, Ti, Zr and Cr within ±0.3 wt% if well-dissolved; (iii) Mg within ±0.5–1.0 wt% due to evaporation; (iv) Zn may lose 1–3 wt%. ICP-OES verification of every powder batch is essential.

**Process-stage seeding.** The NIST AM-Bench 2022 aluminium challenge data provides single-track absorptance and X-ray imaging data for laser melting of bare aluminium plate, useful for calibrating melt-pool models (benoit2026provenancetrackedexperimentallyvalidated pages 61-63). The Barrionuevo et al. AlSi10Mg compilation reportedly aggregates ~270 records spanning laser power, speed, hatch, layer thickness, preheat, density, hardness and tensile properties from multiple studies, providing a useful structured dataset for process–density and process–property surrogate models. Machine-learning-optimized process parameter data for AlSi10Mg (200–355 W, 1307–2320 mm/s, relative densities of 99.2–99.4%) have been reported with Gaussian process regression achieving high accuracy (liu2021machinelearningassistedprocess pages 45-51).

**Property-stage seeding.** Review articles by Aversa et al. (2019) and Liu et al. (2024) contain tabulated tensile data for 10–30+ LPBF Al alloys covering compositions, process conditions, microstructures and mechanical properties, which can be manually digitized for training (he2021designanddevelopment pages 30-35). CALPHAD databases (Thermo-Calc TCAL, Pandat PanAl) can generate arbitrarily large synthetic composition screens of Scheil curves, phase fractions and thermophysical properties for use as low-fidelity training data (hyer2021effectsofalloy pages 1-2, dreano2022computationaldesignof pages 6-9, dreano2022computationaldesignof pages 4-6).

The fuller relation applies corrections for fluid dynamics. A ±20–30% screening uncertainty is prudent because amplitude, film thickness, temperature, oxidation and satellites alter the distribution. (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 4-5) | Seed atomization BO with frequency–temperature–composition predictions; use predicted size as the prior mean and learn residuals for sieve yield and measured distribution quantiles. | Bałasz et al. (2023), [10.5604/01.3001.0016.3393](https://doi.org/10.5604/01.3001.0016.3393) (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 4-5) |


*Table: Physics-based and semi-empirical models for low-fidelity data generation across atomization, print-window, cracking and property stages. The limitations identify where LPBF-aluminium calibration and model-discrepancy treatment are essential.*

**Melt-pool models (Eagar–Tsai, Rosenthal).** The Eagar–Tsai model treats the laser as a moving Gaussian heat source on a semi-infinite body and predicts melt-pool width, depth and temperature field. It is typically accurate to ±20–30% for conduction-mode LPBF after alloy-specific absorptivity calibration, but fails in the keyhole regime because it neglects recoil pressure, Marangoni convection and free-surface depression. McElfresh et al. (2024) used the Eagar–Tsai model as a fast surrogate within a cellular-automaton framework for LPBF microstructure prediction. Lack-of-fusion criteria (pool depth ≥ layer thickness with overlap) and keyhole thresholds (normalized enthalpy or aspect ratio) can be applied to the model outputs to delineate admissible process windows. For LPBF 6061 aluminium, Sonawane (2021) coupled Rosenthal thermal simulations with the RDG hot-cracking criterion and found qualitative agreement between predicted cracking-sensitivity maps and experimental observations (sonawane2021structuralaluminumalloy pages 1-12).

**Scheil-based hot-cracking indices.** The Kou index, defined as |dT/d(f_s^{1/2})| near complete solidification, computed from Scheil–Gulliver curves using CALPHAD databases, has shown good qualitative correlation with experimental LPBF cracking behaviour for binary Al–Si, Al–Mg and Al–Cu alloys (hyer2021effectsofalloy pages 1-2). Hyer et al. (2020) demonstrated that including solid-state diffusion in the Scheil simulation substantially reduces predicted susceptibility and shifts the composition of maximum susceptibility. The Clyne–Davies CSC and Scheil-based brittle-temperature-range (BTR) criteria provide complementary metrics. Dreano et al. (2022) used a genetic algorithm with Scheil-BTR minimization and solid-solution strengthening maximization to computationally design a crack-free Al–6.7Mg–3Si–1.4Ni–1Zn–0.3Fe alloy with a BTR of only 9 °C (dreano2022computationaldesignof pages 22-24, dreano2022computationaldesignof pages 1-4, dreano2022computationaldesignof pages 4-6). Uba et al. (2025) used Kou's HSI criterion and Clyne–Davies CSC in Thermo-Calc to screen modified Al 7xxx compositions for LPBF printability (uba2025enhancingtheprintability pages 4-5).

**Strengthening models.** Solid-solution strengthening using an atomic-size-misfit power law (Δσ_ss ∝ K·ε^{4/3}·c^{2/3}) was applied by Dreano et al. for alloy optimization (dreano2022computationaldesignof pages 6-9). For the Al–Mn–Ti–Zr system, Mair et al. measured that 3.7 wt% Mn in supersaturated solid solution contributed approximately 104 MPa (37% of the 284 MPa yield strength), consistent with the ~30 MPa per wt% Mn literature value (mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 1-2). Orowan precipitation strengthening has been used to predict the aging response of L1₂ Al₃(Sc,Zr) precipitates in Scalmalloy-type alloys and of quasicrystalline particles in Al–Fe–Cr composites (kang2023laserpowderbed pages 1-3). Taheri-Mousavi et al. (2024) used a hybrid ICME + Bayesian-optimization workflow with CALPHAD-derived descriptors including L1₂ phase fraction, coarsening metrics and cracking susceptibility as inputs to a neural-network surrogate, achieving ~3% normalized prediction error with 40 training compositions and using expected-improvement Bayesian optimization to identify an optimized Al–Er–Zr–Ni alloy with 40% higher L1₂ fraction than the initial design (taherimousavi2024additivelymanufacturablehighstrength pages 1-4, taherimousavi2024additivelymanufacturablehighstrength pages 7-9).

**Lang's equation for ultrasonic atomization.** The simplified Lang relation D ≈ 0.34·[8πγ/(ρf²)]^{1/3} predicts the Sauter mean droplet diameter from melt surface tension γ, density ρ and ultrasonic frequency f, with corrections for Weber, Ohnesorge and intensity numbers (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 4-5). Accuracy is approximately ±20–30% for metals. This can seed an atomization-stage BO model predicting sieve yield and particle size distribution as a function of frequency, temperature and composition.

**Key observations.** AlSi10Mg remains the volumetric baseline at approximately 250–350 MPa yield strength as-built, with UTS of 380–450 MPa and elongation of 5–8% (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017). Scalmalloy® achieves 456–469 MPa yield strength after direct aging at 325 °C for 4 h, but relies on ~0.7 wt% Sc (pqac-00000001). Among Sc-free systems, the Al–Mn–Ti–Zr alloy by Mair et al. achieved 284 MPa yield strength and 16.9% elongation as-built through metastable Mn supersaturation and coherent L1₂ Al₃(Ti,Zr) grain refinement (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000024). The A20X-type Al–Cu–TiB₂ alloy reached 401 MPa UTS as-built with 17.7% elongation and 99.5% density, with TiB₂ providing heterogeneous nucleation and sub-micron grain size (pqac-00000005). Near-eutectic Al–10Ce delivered 222 MPa yield strength and 319 MPa UTS with 10.8% elongation, exploiting the thermally stable Al₁₁Ce₃ eutectic (pqac-00000006). Al–Fe–Mg–Zr eutectic alloys reached 376 MPa yield strength after aging at 400 °C for 4 h (pqac-00000022), and Al–Fe–Cr quasicrystal-reinforced composites reached 395 MPa yield strength and 531 MPa UTS, though with limited ductility (pqac-00000023). For inoculated wrought alloys, AA7075 + 1 wt% Zr achieved crack-free builds with 325–373 MPa yield strength (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010), and AA6061 + Zr-based nanoparticles reached 267 MPa UTS with 14.2% elongation and 99.94% density (pqac-00000010).

---

## 2. Recommended Literature-Chosen Seed Compositions

For a campaign whose search space covers Al with additions from {Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce}, four seed compositions are recommended that (i) spread across the composition space, (ii) are dosable from available master alloys and elemental additions, (iii) melt fully at moderate superheat, and (iv) are likely printable without a heated plate:

**Seed 1: Al–10Si–0.35Mg (AlSi10Mg baseline).** This eutectic system is universally printable, requires no heated plate, melts at ~600 °C with minimal superheat, and is dosable from elemental Si and Mg. It anchors the Si-rich corner and serves as the density and cracking benchmark. Extensive literature data exist for model validation (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017).

**Seed 2: Al–4Mn–0.5Ti–0.5Zr (~Mair-type).** Dosable from Al–10Mn, Al–10Ti and Al–10Zr master alloys. The liquidus is only moderately elevated by Mn, Ti and Zr additions (Mn has ~2 wt% equilibrium solubility at ~660 °C, and Ti/Zr additions are small). The alloy prints crack-free without preheat at 380 W / 1900 mm/s with 284 MPa yield strength and excellent 16.9% elongation (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000024). This anchors the Mn-rich, Sc-free transition-metal corner.

**Seed 3: Al–10Ce (near-eutectic).** Dosable from Al–10Ce master alloy. The Al–Ce eutectic at ~10 wt% Ce melts near 640 °C with high fluidity and a narrow freezing range, ensuring crack-free printing without preheat (pqac-00000006). The composition anchors the rare-earth/eutectic corner and provides thermal stability data. Ce is a rare-earth element but substantially more abundant and less supply-critical than Sc or Er.

**Seed 4: Al–4.5Cu–0.3Mg–0.3Ti + 1 vol% TiB₂ (A20X-type).** Dosable from elemental Cu, Mg and Al–Ti–B master alloy or pre-alloyed A20X powder. This anchors the Cu-rich, age-hardenable corner. The TiB₂ grain-refinement strategy produces crack-free, dense parts with 401 MPa UTS and 17.7% elongation as-built (pqac-00000005). The liquidus is below ~650 °C and the alloy prints without preheat.

These four seeds cover the Si, Mn/Cr/Zr, Ce/Fe/Ni and Cu corners of the accessible search space. They avoid clustering, are all achievable by ultrasonic atomization from a 6063 or high-purity Al base with master-alloy dosing, and have demonstrated printability without heated plates.

---

## 3. Atomization Problems and Composition Fidelity

**Droplet size prediction.** For ultrasonic atomization of aluminium alloys at typical operating frequencies of 20–60 kHz, the characteristic droplet diameter can be estimated via the Lang-type relation D₃₂ ≈ 0.34·[8πγ/(ρf²)]^(1/3), where γ is the melt surface tension, ρ is the density and f is the ultrasonic frequency. Corrections based on Weber, Ohnesorge and intensity numbers refine the estimate. Doubling frequency is predicted to reduce powder size by approximately 40% (pqac-00000018). Accuracy is typically ±20–30% for metals when thermophysical properties are well known.

**Mg and Zn evaporation.** Magnesium (boiling point ~1091 °C) and zinc (boiling point ~907 °C) are volatile under the temperatures needed to melt aluminium alloys for atomization and during LPBF processing. Mg loss of 0.5–2 wt% is commonly observed during both gas atomization and LPBF, reducing the effectiveness of Mg₂Si and MgZn₂ precipitation strengthening (pqac-00000019). For alloys targeting >4 wt% Mg (Addalloy-type or Scalmalloy compositions), significant process-stability problems arise from Mg evaporation and spatter during LPBF, which Mair et al. noted as a key reason to favor the Al–Mn system over Al–Mg for Sc-free designs (pqac-00000024). Zn is even more volatile and losses can exceed 1–3 wt% during LPBF, making 7xxx-type compositions especially challenging for composition fidelity.

**Oxide films.** Aluminium readily forms Al₂O₃ films. In small-batch ultrasonic atomization, maintaining inert-atmosphere purity (<100 ppm O₂) is essential. Oxide films on powders increase laser reflectivity, reduce flowability and can create oxide inclusions in printed parts. Charge sizes of 250 g are small enough that oxide-to-volume ratio may be higher than in industrial-scale atomization.

**Primary intermetallics.** High Zr content (>~0.5 wt%) risks formation of primary Al₃Zr during slow cooling of the melt before atomization, which can clog nozzles and produce inhomogeneous powder. The peritectic nature of Al₃Zr (formation at ~660 °C) means that at >1 wt% Zr, significant primary particles form unless extremely rapid quenching occurs. Similarly, Cr has very limited solubility in Al (~0.4 wt% at 660 °C) and can form primary Al₇Cr or Al₁₃Cr₂ intermetallics. Ce and Ni form intermetallics (Al₁₁Ce₃, Al₃Ni) at eutectic compositions, which are actually beneficial for printability but may settle or segregate in the crucible before atomization if the melt superheat is insufficient.

**Composition fidelity expectations.** For the recommended seed compositions atomized in 250 g batches: (i) Si, Cu, Fe, Ni and Ce are expected to be retained within ±0.2 wt% of target; (ii) Mn, Ti, Zr and Cr within ±0.3 wt% if well-dissolved; (iii) Mg within ±0.5–1.0 wt% due to evaporation; (iv) Zn may lose 1–3 wt%. ICP-OES verification of every powder batch is essential.

---

**Process-stage seeding.** The NIST AM-Bench 2022 aluminium challenge data provides single-track absorptance and X-ray imaging data for laser melting of bare aluminium plate, useful for calibrating melt-pool models (pqac-00000011). The Barrionuevo et al. AlSi10Mg compilation reportedly aggregates ~270 records spanning laser power, speed, hatch, layer thickness, preheat, density, hardness and tensile properties from multiple studies, providing a useful structured dataset for process–density and process–property surrogate models. Machine-learning-optimized process parameter data for AlSi10Mg (200–355 W, 1307–2320 mm/s, relative densities of 99.2–99.4%) have been reported with Gaussian process regression achieving high accuracy (pqac-00000015).

**Property-stage seeding.** Review articles by Aversa et al. (2019) and Liu et al. (2024) contain tabulated tensile data for 10–30+ LPBF Al alloys covering compositions, process conditions, microstructures and mechanical properties, which can be manually digitized for training (pqac-00000016). CALPHAD databases (Thermo-Calc TCAL, Pandat PanAl) can generate arbitrarily large synthetic composition screens of Scheil curves, phase fractions and thermophysical properties for use as low-fidelity training data (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029).

---

## 5. Physics-Based and Semi-Empirical Models for Synthetic Data Generation

The following table details models that can generate low-cost "fantasy" data for each stage of the BO pipeline, their accuracy for LPBF aluminium, and how they have been used as priors or low-fidelity sources.

| Model | Pipeline stage | What it predicts | Key inputs | Accuracy / limitations for LPBF Al | Use as BO prior or low-fidelity source | Key reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Eagar–Tsai moving Gaussian heat-source model | Print-parameter stage | Conduction-mode melt-pool width, depth, length and temperature field | Laser power `P`, speed `v`, Gaussian beam radius, effective absorptivity, conductivity, diffusivity, density, heat capacity, liquidus temperature and preheat temperature | Often useful to roughly ±20–30% after alloy- and machine-specific calibration. Fixed absorptivity and constant-property assumptions cause systematic error. It omits recoil pressure, Marangoni flow, evaporation and free-surface depression, so it is unreliable in the keyhole regime. | Evaluate thousands of `P–v` points cheaply; use outputs as GP features, a physics-informed prior mean or the low-fidelity level of a multi-fidelity GP. Recalibrate absorptivity and beam radius from initial single tracks. | McElfresh, Wang and Marian (2024), [10.1016/j.heliyon.2023.e23202](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2023.e23202) |
| Rosenthal analytical moving-source model | Print-parameter stage | Approximate temperature field, cooling rate, thermal gradient and melt-pool isotherm | `P`, `v`, absorptivity, conductivity, diffusivity, initial temperature and liquidus temperature; usually assumes a semi-infinite homogeneous body | Suitable for order-of-magnitude trends and ranking parameter sets, not precise pool geometry. It neglects powder heterogeneity, convection, vaporization and keyholing. For LPBF 6061, coupled thermal and cracking trends agreed qualitatively with experiments. (pqac-00000012) | Generate coarse `P–v–T₀` maps and derived thermal-gradient, cooling-rate and solidification-velocity features; learn experimental residuals rather than treating predictions as equal-fidelity observations. | Sonawane (2021), [10.70675/b76c3001z60daz4747zb50bzf30f70232dcd](https://doi.org/10.70675/b76c3001z60daz4747zb50bzf30f70232dcd) (pqac-00000012) |
| Geometric lack-of-fusion and keyhole criteria | Print-parameter stage | Classification or probability of lack of fusion, conduction mode, keyholing and an admissible process window | Predicted pool depth and width, layer thickness, hatch spacing, beam radius, packing fraction, overlap criterion and keyhole aspect-ratio or normalized-enthalpy threshold | Efficiently delineates broad defect regimes, but transition boundaries are approximate and machine dependent. Aluminium absorptivity changes with temperature, oxide condition and keyhole formation, so thresholds need single-track calibration. | Apply as probabilistic feasibility constraints with uncertain thresholds; use distance from each defect boundary as surrogate-model features. | King et al. (pqac-00000013) | Screen large composition libraries; use the normalized index as a GP feature, low-fidelity objective or probabilistic crack constraint. *Table: Physics-based and semi-empirical models for low-fidelity data generation across atomization, print-window, cracking and property stages. The limitations identify where LPBF-aluminium calibration and model-discrepancy treatment are essential.*

**Melt-pool models (Eagar–Tsai, Rosenthal).** The Eagar–Tsai model treats the laser as a moving Gaussian heat source on a semi-infinite body and predicts melt-pool width, depth and temperature field. It is typically accurate to ±20–30% for conduction-mode LPBF after alloy-specific absorptivity calibration, but fails in the keyhole regime because it neglects recoil pressure, Marangoni convection and free-surface depression. McElfresh et al. (2024) used the Eagar–Tsai model as a fast surrogate within a cellular-automaton framework for LPBF microstructure prediction. Lack-of-fusion criteria (pool depth ≥ layer thickness with overlap) and keyhole thresholds (normalized enthalpy or aspect ratio) can be applied to the model outputs to delineate admissible process windows. For LPBF 6061 aluminium, Sonawane (2021) coupled Rosenthal thermal simulations with the RDG hot-cracking criterion and found qualitative agreement between predicted cracking-sensitivity maps and experimental observations (pqac-00000012).

**Scheil-based hot-cracking indices.** The Kou index, defined as |dT/d(f_s^{1/2})| near complete solidification, computed from Scheil–Gulliver curves using CALPHAD databases, has shown good qualitative correlation with experimental LPBF cracking behaviour for binary Al–Si, Al–Mg and Al–Cu alloys (pqac-00000013). Hyer et al. (2020) demonstrated that including solid-state diffusion in the Scheil simulation substantially reduces predicted susceptibility and shifts the composition of maximum susceptibility. The Clyne–Davies CSC and Scheil-based brittle-temperature-range (BTR) criteria provide complementary metrics. Dreano et al. (2022) used a genetic algorithm with Scheil-BTR minimization and solid-solution strengthening maximization to computationally design a crack-free Al–6.7Mg–3Si–1.4Ni–1Zn–0.3Fe alloy with a BTR of only 9 °C (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). Uba et al. (2025) used Kou's HSI criterion and Clyne–Davies CSC in Thermo-Calc to screen modified Al 7xxx compositions for LPBF printability (pqac-00000030).

**Strengthening models.** Solid-solution strengthening using an atomic-size-misfit power law (Δσ_ss ∝ K·ε^{4/3}·c^{2/3}) was applied by Dreano et al. for alloy optimization (pqac-00000027). For the Al–Mn–Ti–Zr system, Mair et al. measured that 3.7 wt% Mn in supersaturated solid solution contributed approximately 104 MPa (37% of the 284 MPa yield strength), consistent with the ~30 MPa per wt% Mn literature value (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000024). Orowan precipitation strengthening has been used to predict the aging response of L1₂ Al₃(Sc,Zr) precipitates in Scalmalloy-type alloys and of quasicrystalline particles in Al–Fe–Cr composites (pqac-00000023). Taheri-Mousavi et al. (2024) used a hybrid ICME + Bayesian-optimization workflow with CALPHAD-derived descriptors including L1₂ phase fraction, coarsening metrics and cracking susceptibility as inputs to a neural-network surrogate, achieving ~3% normalized prediction error with 40 training compositions and using expected-improvement Bayesian optimization to identify an optimized Al–Er–Zr–Ni alloy with 40% higher L1₂ fraction than the initial design (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

**Lang's equation for ultrasonic atomization.** The simplified Lang relation D ≈ 0.34·[8πγ/(ρf²)]^{1/3} predicts the Sauter mean droplet diameter from melt surface tension γ, density ρ and ultrasonic frequency f, with corrections for Weber, Ohnesorge and intensity numbers (pqac-00000018). Accuracy is approximately ±20–30% for metals. This can seed an atomization-stage BO model predicting sieve yield and particle size distribution as a function of frequency, temperature and composition.

For heat-treated material, the reported room-temperature ultimate tensile strength is up to 560.6 MPa with 11.1% elongation. Strength is slightly higher in the H direction than in the Z direction, with less than a 5% difference. With increasing temperature, the reported strength/elongation pairs are 435.1 MPa/25.8% at 100 °C, 269.4 MPa/20.1% at 150 °C, 102.8 MPa/47.9% at 200 °C, and 54.0 MPa/72.2% at 250 °C, indicating reduced strength and generally increased ductility at elevated temperature. The microstructure consists of aligned melt pools with fine equiaxed boundary grains and larger equiaxed interior grains, forming a bimodal structure. The excerpt suggests resistance to brittle failure through this refined microstructure and Al3(Sc,Zr) precipitates, while fracture remains predominantly ductile and dimpled. It does not explicitly identify cracking-suppression mechanisms.

snippets: Room-temperature tensile tests demonstrated that the heat-treated specimens achieved ultimate tensile strengths up to 560.6 MPa, coupled with an elongation of 11.1%.
Tensile strengths for both untreated and treated samples were modestly higher in the H direction than in the Z direction, with the discrepancy being less than 5%.

The microstructure is characterized by neatly aligned melt pools, with the boundaries marked by fine equiaxed grains and the interiors by larger equiaxed grains, creating a distinct bimodal distribution.
Fracture surface analyses from tensile tests across the temperature range disclosed an abundance of dimples, indicative of ductile fracture behavior.
The dimples are mainly attributed to the presence of the second-phase Al3(Sc, Zr) particles.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides data only for the Ti- and Zr-modified Al-Mn alloy, not for AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy, Al-Ce, Al-Cu-TiB2 (A20X), Al-Mg-Zr (Addalloy), 7075+Zr, or 6061+Zr. For the Al-Mn-Ti-Zr alloy fabricated by LPBF, the as-built mechanical properties are a yield strength of 284 ± 3 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 320 ± 1 MPa, and elongation at fracture of 16.9 ± 0.2%. The reported optimized process parameters are 380 W laser power, 1900 mm/s scanning speed, 100 µm hatch distance, 30 µm layer thickness, and no substrate preheating (0 °C implied by the stated condition). Potential cracking-suppression mechanisms described in the excerpt include LPBF’s high cooling rate and temperature gradient, which increase solute retention and promote metastable phases; Ti/Zr-bearing primary Al3(Ti,Zr) nanoparticles provide efficient heterogeneous nucleation through a highly coherent interface with α-Al; and the resulting fine equiaxed grain regions contribute to grain refinement alongside coarse columnar regions. The excerpt does not explicitly report cracking results or mechanisms for the other requested alloys.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not provide alloy-specific mechanical-property values or processing-parameter tables for AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy, Al-Mn-Ti-Zr, Al-Ce, Al-Cu-TiB2 (A20X), Al-Mg-Zr (Addalloy), 7075+Zr, or 6061+Zr. It does, however, describe general LPBF relationships relevant to those alloys. Laser power and scan speed control melt-pool dimensions, while hatch spacing and scan strategy affect melting, welding, solidification, densification, residual stress, and final microstructure. Complex or varying scan strategies can improve densification and reduce residual stresses; simple strategies may produce lack of fusion, porosity, and unwelded regions. LPBF’s high cooling rates promote refined microstructures, metastable phases, and supersaturated solid solutions. Heat extraction toward the substrate commonly produces directional columnar grains, while scanning direction influences grain-growth orientation. High thermal stresses associated with low scan speeds and high energy input can cause cracking when residual stress exceeds the material’s strength. Columnar grains reduce strain accommodation and liquid permeability between grains, increasing hot-cracking susceptibility. The excerpt does not discuss hatch distance, layer thickness, preheating temperature, elongation, yield strength, UTS, or specific crack-suppression alloying mechanisms for the listed alloys.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides data primarily for LPBF Scalmalloy®, not for AlSi10Mg, Al-Mn-Ti-Zr, Al-Ce, Al-Cu-TiB2 (A20X), Al-Mg-Zr (Addalloy), 7075+Zr, or 6061+Zr. For as-built Scalmalloy®, reported yield strength is 256–278 MPa, UTS is 349–350 MPa, and elongation is 19.0–20.0%. Direct aging at 325 °C for 4 h raises yield strength to 456–469 MPa and UTS to 512–521 MPa, while reducing elongation to 12.0–13.0%. HIP at 325 °C for 4 h and 1000 bar reduces porosity to approximately 0.18% and gives yield strength of 482–493 MPa and UTS of 523–547 MPa. The stated LPBF process parameters are laser power, scan speed, hatch distance, and layer thickness, related through VED = P/(vht); no numerical parameter values or preheat temperature are given in this excerpt. Cracking suppression mechanisms identified for Scalmalloy® include Al3Sc seed crystals that promote heterogeneous nucleation and grain refinement, and Zr-stabilized Al3(Sc,Zr) precipitates that resist coarsening and recrystallization. The excerpt does not provide comparative mechanical properties, process settings, preheat temperatures, or cracking mechanisms for the other listed alloys.

The excerpt also notes general aluminum-processing challenges, including poor powder flowability, high reflectivity and thermal conductivity requiring high laser power, and oxide films that reduce wettability and remelting and can cause porosity. LPBF cooling rates of 10^3–10^6 K/s generate fine cellular/dendritic microstructures, while AlSi10Mg mechanical performance is attributed to eutectic-cell-boundary Hall–Petch strengthening, Orowan strengthening from Si and Mg2Si, and dislocation hardening. contexts.context: The excerpt provides mechanical-property information primarily for LPBF near-eutectic Al-Ce alloys. Binary Al-10Ce is reported with approximately 222 MPa yield strength, 319 MPa ultimate tensile strength, and 10.8% elongation at break. Al-Ce alloys exhibit high temperature stability because Ce has very low solubility and diffusion in aluminum; Al11Ce3 precipitates during solidification and remains resistant to dissolution and coarsening. Near-eutectic Al-Ce compositions reportedly have high melt fluidity and a wide process-parameter range for producing crack-free samples. The excerpt explains that LPBF microstructure depends on laser-processing-induced temperature gradient, solidification rate, and undercooling, with commonly observed columnar and equiaxed structures. It does not provide numerical laser power, scan speed, hatch distance, or relative-density values for Al-Ce. It also does not contain data on Al-Fe-Ni, Al-Cu-Mg with TiB2/A20X, Al-Mg-Zr Addalloy, or 7075/6061 alloys with Zr or TiB2 inoculation, nor does it describe their specific cracking mechanisms. The only general cracking discussion attributes cracking susceptibility in conventional high-strength 2xxx, 6xxx, and 7xxx alloys to non-equilibrium LPBF cooling, while near-eutectic Al-Si compositions reduce the liquidus-solidus interval and improve crack-free processing.

It does provide general process and cracking mechanisms relevant to comparing these alloy systems. Laser power and scanning speed control molten-pool dimensions, while hatch spacing and scanning strategy affect melting, welding, solidification, microstructure, densification, and residual stress. Complex strategies such as chessboard or changing scan directions can improve homogeneity and reduce residual stresses, whereas simple strategies may cause lack of fusion and porosity. LPBF’s high cooling rates produce refined and sometimes metastable microstructures, while directional heat extraction promotes columnar grains. Hot cracking is associated with thermal and residual stresses generated during solidification and contraction; cracking occurs when stresses exceed material strength. Columnar grains reduce strain accommodation and liquid permeability between grains, increasing hot-cracking susceptibility, particularly in wrought aluminum alloys because insufficient liquid remains during final solidification to fill interdendritic voids.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides information only for LPBF processing of AA7075 modified with elemental Zr; it does not report the requested mechanical properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, or elongation), relative density, or explicit numerical values for laser power, scan speed, or hatch distance. The study varied laser power and scanning speed through volumetric energy density (VED) to obtain crack-free parts. A 1 wt.% Zr addition produced lower crack density than 0.3 wt.% Zr, and crack-free components were achieved at high VED. The proposed cracking mitigation mechanism is microstructural refinement: Al3Zr promotes nucleation of fine equiaxed aluminum grains at the molten-pool boundary rather than large columnar grains, helping suppress solidification cracks. Solidification cracking is attributed to shrinkage and thermal stresses during the final stage of solidification, when liquid films between dendrites tear and liquid feeding is poor. Silicon segregation near cracks persisted after Zr modification, although its cracking effect was reduced. Zr also increased spherical porosity because unmelted particles reduced melt fluidity and disrupted Marangoni flow; sufficient laser energy improved pore escape. The excerpt contains no data on Al-Ce, Al-Fe-Ni, Al-Cu-Mg/TiB2 (A20X), Al-Mg-Zr Addalloy, or 6061 with Zr/TiB2.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides information primarily on Scheil–Gulliver solidification analysis and Kou’s hot-cracking criterion for LPBF aluminium alloy design. Kou’s criterion treats solidification-cracking susceptibility as proportional to the absolute steepness of the temperature versus the square root of fraction solidified curve, |dT/dfS1/2|, as complete solidification is approached. The article applies this approach to binary Al–Si, Al–Mg, and Al–Cu alloys and evaluates susceptibility as a function of solute concentration. Conventional Scheil–Gulliver assumptions include complete diffusion in the liquid and no diffusion in the solid; introducing solid-state diffusion substantially reduces the predicted cracking susceptibility and shifts the composition of maximum susceptibility toward higher solute concentrations. The authors report good correlation between calculated susceptibility and LPBF experiments on AA5083 and Al–Si alloys with varying silicon content. The excerpt also emphasizes that diffusion effects depend on cooling rate and total freezing time, and therefore may be especially important for LPBF’s very rapid cooling rates (approximately 10^5–10^7 K/s). It does not provide information about the quantitative accuracy of Eagar–Tsai or Rosenthal melt-pool models, their use as Bayesian-optimization priors or low-fidelity sources, or the accuracy of solid-solution, precipitation/Orowan, or Hall–Petch strengthening models.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides limited but relevant evidence concerning Scheil-based solidification analysis and alloy-design objectives for LPBF aluminium. The authors use a Scheil model to interpret phase formation during solidification: Mg2Si is predicted to form jointly with the FCC alpha-Al phase from approximately 29% solid fraction, while Al9FeNi is associated with interdendritic segregation and formation near the end of solidification. Powder microstructure observations and EDX mapping support these assignments, with Mg and Si enriched in dark domains identified as Mg2Si and Fe/Ni enriched in brighter interdendritic domains associated with Al9FeNi. The paper also notes that the alloy exhibited low ductility related to porosity and secondary phases that reduced cohesion between seams. It proposes extending the computational design algorithm with objective functions describing the nature of intermetallic phases and their ability to dissolve or precipitate during annealing or aging, thereby optimizing mechanical properties. These additions would improve alloy-selection relevance but increase multi-objective algorithm complexity. However, this excerpt contains no quantitative validation of Eagar-Tsai or Rosenthal melt-pool model accuracy, no discussion of their use as Bayesian-optimization priors or low-fidelity models, no explicit Kou hot-cracking-index results, and no numerical accuracy assessment for solid-solution, precipitation/Orowan, or Hall-Petch strengthening models.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not provide accuracy assessments for the Eagar–Tsai or Rosenthal melt-pool models, nor does it describe their use as priors or low-fidelity sources in Bayesian optimization. It also does not specifically discuss Scheil solidification combined with the Kou hot-cracking index. Instead, it presents a computational alloy-design framework for LPBF aluminum that uses thermodynamic and property-based criteria in an aggregated genetic algorithm. The central hot-cracking strategy is to reduce the brittle temperature range (BTR), which represents the temperature interval of greatest susceptibility to hot cracking. The design also imposes criteria related to phase fractions, solid-solution strengthening, mechanical strength, and ductility. CALPHAD is identified as a method capable of predicting microstructure, precipitation, and phases, but no quantitative validation accuracy is reported in the excerpt. The resulting candidate alloy was predicted to have a BTR of 9°C, approximately 90% FCC phase, and Mg2Si and Al9FeNi precipitates; LPBF experiments found no cracks, supporting the BTR-based design criterion. Mechanical testing showed high yield and ultimate tensile strengths, but relatively low elongation compared with conventionally manufactured aluminum alloys. No quantitative accuracy information is given for solid-solution, precipitation/Orowan, or Hall–Petch strengthening models.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports the use of Lang’s model for estimating droplet size in ultrasonic atomization of molten metals, including aluminium alloys. The reported relation is D32 = 0.34·λ·f(We, Oh, In), where λ is the capillary-wave length and the correction function depends on Weber, Ohnesorge, and ultrasonic-intensity numbers. For preliminary estimates, the expression is simplified using molten-metal surface tension, density, and ultrasonic frequency; the resulting droplet dimensions are then scaled for thermal contraction during cooling. The article states that the measured average powder diameter is nearly equal to D32. It identifies ultrasonic frequency and atomization temperature as the principal variables: doubling frequency is predicted to reduce powder size by approximately 40%, while temperature changes affect surface tension and density. The process uses electric-arc heating in an inert atmosphere, and unstable capillary waves eject molten droplets that become spherical through surface tension before solidifying. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a hybrid alloy-design workflow combining CALPHAD/ICME simulations, Bayesian optimization, and machine-learning analysis to search a multidimensional composition space efficiently. The design targets were linked to microstructural and processing constraints: rapid-solidification formation of submicron metastable ternary phases, subsequent nanoscale L12 Al3M precipitation, low L12 coarsening rates for thermal stability, reduced fractions of fast-growing phases, and controlled solidification temperature ranges and times to suppress LPBF hot cracking. The selected model alloy was based on the Al-Er-Zr-Y-Yb-Ni system. Rapid solidification during LPBF was intended to create fine Al-Ni-M ternary phases that act as sources for thermally stable Al3M (L12) nanoprecipitates during heat treatment. The resulting LPBF alloy had strength comparable to wrought Al 7075 without its cracking problem, and after aging at 400°C it was reported to be 50% stronger than the strongest benchmark printable aluminum alloy. The supplied pages do not provide the exact optimized elemental composition, numerical yield strengths, or detailed CALPHAD Scheil outputs; they only identify the alloy family and relative performance. They also state that slower-solidified control material produced much coarser phases and approximately five-times-lower hardness.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a hybrid data-driven/ICME workflow for designing additively manufactured Al alloys. First, CALPHAD-derived microstructural descriptors—particularly the L12 phase fraction, phase size, coarsening metric, cracking susceptibility, and fraction of adverse phases—were analyzed using Spearman correlations. Because these relationships were nonlinear, the authors trained and compared six surrogate-modeling methods using alloy composition (the atomic percentages of five elements) as inputs. A neural-network surrogate performed best, reaching approximately 3% normalized prediction error with 40 compositions, and was used as a forward model linking composition to coarsening behavior. For inverse design, Bayesian optimization employed a Gaussian-process surrogate, Latin-hypercube sampling, and expected improvement to balance exploration and exploitation. Objectives included maximizing L12 content, minimizing coarsening, and imposing constraints related to Er and Zr and printability. The design analysis found that Zr lowers coarsening through partitioning and low diffusivity, while Er promotes L12 formation and enables Zr incorporation into stable strengthening phases; omitting Er could instead produce brittle Al3Zr. The excerpt reports an optimized alloy with 40% higher L12 fraction and a 3.5-fold lower coarsening metric while satisfying printability, but it does not provide the alloy’s exact composition or yield strength. Detailed strengthening-model implementation and final yield-strength values are also absent from these pages.

(Additive Manufacturing 55, 102876, 2022, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2022.102876) computationally optimized LPBF aluminium using CALPHAD-derived brittle-temperature range (BTR), phase fractions, and solid-solution strengthening in a genetic algorithm.
